question_text: A 63-year-old woman with a previous diagnosis of rheumatoid arthritis and Sjogren syndrome was referred for a second opinion. She has had a known chronic idiopathic pericardial effusion for about a year and has dealt with intermittent chest pain ever since. She underwent 2 diagnostic pericardiocenteses, but the fluid returned each time. She also has used empiric anti-inflammatory therapies with NSAIDs and colchicine without significant changes in the size of the pericardial effusion. The etiological testing was negative. At this visit, she is still complaining of pain in her chest but has no evidence of distended neck veins. An ECG shows sinus rhythm with low QRS voltages. What will be the procedure of choice that would be both therapeutic and diagnostic?
